common_name: Gallery Pablo Dahlia (Dwarf Patio Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep after the last frost; Gallery Pablo is a dwarf decorative dahlia bred for pots and border fronts, producing showy light coral-red blooms shading to apricot-yellow at the petal base.

directions: Plant tubers four to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the danger of frost has passed. Gallery Pablo is a compact, dwarf decorative dahlia from the Dutch-bred Gallery series, named for painters and art movements, bearing freely produced light coral-red flowers roughly six inches across that shade to apricot-yellow near the base of each petal. Its low, bushy habit needs no staking and suits containers, window boxes, and the front of mixed borders, flowering continuously from midsummer until frost if spent blooms are deadheaded regularly. In frost-free zones the tubers can be left in the ground with heavy mulch, while gardeners farther north should lift and store them indoors over winter.

common_name: Gallery Serenade Dahlia (Dwarf Patio Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep after the last frost; Gallery Serenade is a dwarf decorative dahlia in the same bedding series as Gallery Pablo, bearing pale lemon-yellow blooms that fade to soft yellow at the petal tips.

directions: Set tubers four to six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above freezing. Gallery Serenade is a dwarf, free-flowering decorative dahlia that opens pale lemon-yellow blooms about five inches wide, the color softening to a gentler yellow toward the petal tips, on a tidy, self-supporting plant well suited to patio containers and the front of sunny beds. It flowers in heavy flushes from midsummer through the first hard frost and responds well to regular deadheading, which keeps fresh buds coming rather than letting the plant set seed. Where winters are too cold for tubers to overwinter outdoors, lift the clumps after the foliage is blackened by frost and store them in a cool, frost-free place until spring.

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Christmas Carol is a collarette dahlia with a single outer ring of bright red florets surrounding a shorter inner collar of creamy-white petals around a yellow disc.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally four to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost. Christmas Carol is a collarette dahlia, a distinctive open-centered form with a single outer ring of flat, bright red ray florets and a shorter inner collar of ruffled, creamy-white petals framing a yellow central disc, giving each flower a two-tone, festive look. The clump-forming plant stays a manageable two to three feet tall with dark green, serrated foliage, blooming steadily from midsummer into autumn and making an excellent cut flower since collarette types hold up well once picked. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and deadhead spent blooms to keep new buds forming through the season.

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Myrtle's Folly is a large laciniated (fringed) collarette dahlia with twisted, split petal tips blending peach, pink, mauve, and orange tones on a tall plant that benefits from staking.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally four to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the danger of frost has passed. Myrtle's Folly produces large, eight-inch blooms with narrow, twisted, laciniated petals that split and fringe at the tips, blending shifting tones of peach, pink, mauve, and soft orange for an unusually textured, shaggy flower. The tall, vigorous plant reaches three and a half to four feet and should be staked early to support the heavy flower heads; pinching the central growing tip once the plant is about a foot tall encourages a bushier habit with more flowering stems. In most regions the tubers need to be lifted after frost blackens the foliage and stored indoors over winter, since this cultivar is reliably hardy outdoors only in the mildest zones.

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Jowey Linda is a ball-type dahlia, part of the Jowey series, with perfectly spherical, fully double apricot-orange blooms on a tall, sturdy plant.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally four to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost. Jowey Linda belongs to the ball-type class of dahlias, forming densely packed, globe-shaped flowers five to six inches across in a warm apricot-orange, held on straight, dark stems that make it a favorite for cutting gardens. The tall plant, reaching upward of three feet, flowers prolifically from midsummer until the first hard frost and pairs well with late-season asters and ornamental grasses in a mixed border. Stake the stems early in the season to keep the heavy, perfectly round blooms upright, and lift and store tubers indoors over winter in all but the mildest climates.

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Yellow Star is a long-popular semi-cactus dahlia with narrow, quilled golden-yellow petals giving the bloom a starburst look, on a tall plant good for cutting.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally four to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost. Yellow Star is a long-cherished semi-cactus dahlia whose narrow, pointed, quilled golden-yellow petals radiate outward in a starburst pattern, forming blooms roughly five to six inches across atop long, sturdy stems well suited to cutting. The vigorous plant can reach four feet and flowers heavily from midsummer through frost, holding its bright, clear yellow color well even in late-season heat. Stake the tall stems to keep the sizable flowers from toppling, deadhead regularly to extend bloom, and lift tubers for winter storage wherever the ground freezes.

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Comet is an anemone-flowered heirloom dahlia with a domed, pincushion-like ruby-red center ringed by a single row of flat ray florets.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally four to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost. Comet is an heirloom anemone-flowered dahlia, a distinctive class in which a dense, domed cushion of tubular disc florets rises from the center of the flower, surrounded by a single outer ring of broader, flat ray florets; in Comet's case both the cushion and ring glow a rich ruby-red with an iridescent sheen on the petal backs. The bushy, medium-height plant produces blooms four to six inches across in generous flushes from midsummer into fall, resembling a fluffy gerbera daisy more than a typical dahlia. Pinch young plants to promote branching, stake if grown in windy sites, and lift tubers for winter storage outside the mildest zones.

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Lambada is an anemone-flowered dahlia with informal pink-and-white outer petals surrounding a raised yellow pincushion center.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally four to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost. Lambada is an anemone-flowered dahlia with an informal, loosely arranged outer skirt of soft pink petals washing to white toward the base, surrounding a raised, golden-yellow pincushion center that gives the bloom real depth and movement. Compact at around two feet tall, it fits well toward the middle of a mixed border without needing heavy staking, though light support helps keep the flowering stems upright in exposed sites. Deadhead spent flowers regularly to prolong the midsummer-to-frost bloom season, and lift tubers for frost-free winter storage outside the warmest growing zones.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Moonbeam is a hardy garden mum of classic pompon form, densely packed with rounded, slightly curled solid-white petals.

directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil. Moonbeam is a true pompon-form chrysanthemum, its densely packed, rounded petals curling inward to build a tidy, nearly spherical, solid-white flower up to four inches across, held well above the dark green foliage on upright stems. Unlike disposable florist pot mums, it is a genuinely hardy garden perennial that returns reliably for years when given good winter drainage, making it a dependable source of crisp white fall color and a long-lasting cut flower. Pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to build a bushy, well-branched plant, and divide congested clumps every two to three years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring; Kermit is a heirloom button-pompon chrysanthemum with bright chartreuse-green petals and emerald-green centers, grown as a half-hardy perennial in mild winters and mulched heavily or treated as tender farther north.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, spacing plants to allow good air movement around the foliage. Kermit is a distinctive heirloom garden chrysanthemum prized for its unusual color: small, fully double, pompon-shaped flowers in bright chartreuse green with a slightly deeper emerald center, blooming on sturdy stems that need little support. Cooler autumn nights intensify the green tones, making it a sought-after novelty for fall cutting gardens and arrangements. Because it is only reliably winter-hardy where winters stay mild, gardeners in colder regions should either grow it as a tender annual, take cuttings to overwinter indoors, or apply a heavy winter mulch and accept that survival is not guaranteed; pinching stem tips through early summer keeps the plant full and well-branched.
